exercises.label: Exercise C.R1 — Readiness: Translate a complement

exercise.html:
Exercise C.R1 — Readiness: Translate a complement

An event $A$ has probability $0.15$. What is the probability that it does not occur? If $A$ means a constraint is violated, which event describes no violation?

Review if needed: sets and complements.

Show hint
An event and its complement partition all outcomes.
Show worked solution

The complement $A^c$ contains exactly the outcomes outside $A$. Since the probabilities of these disjoint events add to $1$, $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-0.15=0.85$. If $A$ means violation, $A^c$ means no violation. This statement concerns the specified event; a guarantee across many times requires defining an event for the whole trajectory.

exercises.label: Exercise C.R2 — Readiness: Build a weighted average

exercise.html:
Exercise C.R2 — Readiness: Build a weighted average

A quantity is $2$ in one quarter of cases and $6$ in the other three quarters. Find the average. Why is simply adding $2+6$ incorrect?

Review if needed: sums and weights.

Show hint
Give each value a weight equal to its fraction of cases.
Show worked solution

In four representative cases the values are $2,6,6,6$, whose average is $(2+6+6+6)/4=5$. Equivalently, $2(1/4)+6(3/4)=5$. Adding $2+6$ ignores both frequencies and the division by the number of cases. An expectation is this same weighted-average idea applied to a probability law.

exercises.label: Exercise C.R3 — Readiness: Check an outer product

exercise.html:
Exercise C.R3 — Readiness: Check an outer product

For column vector $v=(1,2)^\top$, compute $vv^\top$ and show that its quadratic form is nonnegative for every vector $w=(w_1,w_2)^\top$.

Review if needed: outer products and PSD matrices.

Show hint
The entry in row $i$, column $j$ is $v_iv_j$. Use $w^\top vv^\top w=(v^\top w)^2$.
Show worked solution

Multiply a column by a row: the entry in position $(i,j)$ is $v_iv_j$. Here this gives

$$vv^\top= \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&2\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot1&1\cdot2\\2\cdot1&2\cdot2\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}.$$

The matrix is symmetric. To check positive semidefiniteness, take an arbitrary $w=(w_1,w_2)^\top$, multiply, and collect the terms:

$$w^\top vv^\top w=w_1^2+4w_1w_2+4w_2^2=(w_1+2w_2)^2\ge0.$$

This works for every $w$, which is exactly the required quadratic-form condition. It does not make the matrix positive definite: $w=(-2,1)^\top$ is nonzero but gives $(-2+2)^2=0$. More generally, $w^\top vv^\top w=(v^\top w)^2$; averages of these nonnegative quantities explain why covariance matrices are positive semidefinite.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S1 — Easy: Read a probability table

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S1 — Easy: Read a probability table

A random cost $X$ is $0$, $2$, or $4$ with probabilities $1/2$, $1/4$, and $1/4$. Check that this is a probability law. Find $\mathbb P(X\ge2)$ and $\mathbb E[X]$.

Review if needed: this section and sets and events.

Show hint
Probabilities add over distinct outcomes. For the mean, multiply each value by its probability before adding.
Show worked solution

A discrete probability law must assign nonnegative weights whose total is one. All three weights are nonnegative, and

$$\frac12+\frac14+\frac14=\frac24+\frac14+\frac14=1.$$

The event $X\ge2$ includes the two distinct outcomes $2$ and $4$. Their events are disjoint, so their probabilities add:

$$\mathbb P(X\ge2)=\mathbb P(X=2)+\mathbb P(X=4)=\frac14+\frac14=\frac12.$$

For the mean, multiply each value by its probability, including the zero outcome:

$$\mathbb E[X]=0\left(\frac12\right)+2\left(\frac14\right)+4\left(\frac14\right) =0+\frac12+1=\frac32.$$

The mean is $1.5$, even though the cost can only be $0$, $2$ or $4$. An expectation describes a weighted average, not an additional possible outcome.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S2 — Medium: Variance is an average of squared distances

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S2 — Medium: Variance is an average of squared distances

For the same law, compute $\mathbb E[X^2]$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and the standard deviation. If $Y=3X+1$, find its mean and variance.

Review if needed: this section and sets and events.

Show hint
Square the values before averaging. A shift changes the mean but leaves distances from the mean unchanged.
Show worked solution

Use the law from the preceding exercise, whose mean is $m=\mathbb E[X]=3/2$. For the second moment, square each possible value before weighting:

$$\mathbb E[X^2]=0^2\left(\frac12\right)+2^2\left(\frac14\right)+4^2\left(\frac14\right) =0+\frac44+\frac{16}4=5.$$

The variance is the average squared distance from the mean. Expanding that square gives $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-m^2$, so

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=5-\left(\frac32\right)^2=\frac{20}4-\frac94=\frac{11}4=2.75, \qquad \operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\frac{11}4}=\frac{\sqrt{11}}2\approx1.658.$$

For $Y=3X+1$, linearity of expectation gives $\mathbb E[Y]=3(3/2)+1=9/2+2/2=11/2$. The constant shift disappears when we subtract this new mean:

$$Y-\mathbb E[Y]=3X+1-\left(3\mathbb E[X]+1\right)=3(X-\mathbb E[X]).$$

Squaring multiplies the distances by $9$, and then averaging gives $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=9\operatorname{Var}(X)=99/4=24.75$. A shift changes the mean; scaling changes the variance by the square of the scale.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S3 — Hard: A covariance calculation that detects dependence

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S3 — Hard: A covariance calculation that detects dependence

Let $X$ be uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$ and set $Y=X^2$. Compute the covariance matrix of $(X,Y)$. Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?

Review if needed: this section and sets and events.

Show hint
Compute $\mathbb E[X]$, $\mathbb E[Y]$, $\mathbb E[XY]$ and both variances. Independence is stronger than covariance zero.
Show worked solution

Each of $X=-1,0,1$ has probability $1/3$, and $Y=X^2$ is respectively $1,0,1$. Compute the means and the cross moment from those three possibilities:

$$\mathbb E[X]=\frac{-1+0+1}{3}=0,\qquad \mathbb E[Y]=\frac{1+0+1}{3}=\frac23,\qquad \mathbb E[XY]=\mathbb E[X^3]=\frac{-1+0+1}{3}=0.$$

Thus $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]=0$. The diagonal entries need the two variances. Since $\mathbb E[X^2]=2/3$ and $Y^2=Y$ for the values $0,1$,

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac23-0^2=\frac23,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac23-\left(\frac23\right)^2=\frac69-\frac49=\frac29.$$

The covariance matrix is consequently $\begin{bmatrix}2/3&0\\0&2/9\end{bmatrix}$. Nevertheless, the variables are dependent. In particular, $Y=0$ occurs exactly when $X=0$, so $\mathbb P(X=0\mid Y=0)=1$, whereas $\mathbb P(X=0)=1/3$. Independence would require these probabilities to agree. Covariance zero detects the absence of this linear association; it does not rule out the nonlinear relation $Y=X^2$.

solution.html:
Each of $X=-1,0,1$ has probability $1/3$, and $Y=X^2$ is respectively $1,0,1$. Compute the means and the cross moment from those three possibilities:

$$\mathbb E[X]=\frac{-1+0+1}{3}=0,\qquad \mathbb E[Y]=\frac{1+0+1}{3}=\frac23,\qquad \mathbb E[XY]=\mathbb E[X^3]=\frac{-1+0+1}{3}=0.$$

Thus $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]=0$. The diagonal entries need the two variances. Since $\mathbb E[X^2]=2/3$ and $Y^2=Y$ for the values $0,1$,

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac23-0^2=\frac23,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac23-\left(\frac23\right)^2=\frac69-\frac49=\frac29.$$

The covariance matrix is consequently $\begin{bmatrix}2/3&0\\0&2/9\end{bmatrix}$. Nevertheless, the variables are dependent. In particular, $Y=0$ occurs exactly when $X=0$, so $\mathbb P(X=0\mid Y=0)=1$, whereas $\mathbb P(X=0)=1/3$. Independence would require these probabilities to agree. Covariance zero detects the absence of this linear association; it does not rule out the nonlinear relation $Y=X^2$.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S4 — Easy: Restrict and renormalise

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S4 — Easy: Restrict and renormalise

Roll a fair six-sided die. Let $A$ mean an even result and $B$ mean a result greater than $3$. Find $\mathbb P(A)$, $\mathbb P(B)$ and $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$.

Review if needed: this section and weighted expectations.

Show hint
Inside $B$, the remaining equally likely results are $4,5,6$.
Show worked solution

For a fair die, each of the six outcomes has probability $1/6$. The events are $A=\{2,4,6\}$ and $B=\{4,5,6\}$, so $\mathbb P(A)=3/6=1/2$ and $\mathbb P(B)=3/6=1/2$.

To have both an even result and a result greater than $3$, the outcome must be $4$ or $6$. Therefore $A\cap B=\{4,6\}$ and $\mathbb P(A\cap B)=2/6$. Since $\mathbb P(B)>0$, conditioning is well defined:

$$\mathbb P(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)} =\frac{2/6}{3/6}=\frac26\frac63=\frac23.$$

Equivalently, after learning $B$, only the equally likely outcomes $4,5,6$ remain; two of those three are even. Conditioning changes the reference group, which is why the answer differs from the unconditional probability $1/2$.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S5 — Medium: Bayes by counting imaginary runs

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S5 — Medium: Bayes by counting imaginary runs

A fault occurs in $10\%$ of runs. An alarm fires on $80\%$ of faulty runs and $20\%$ of healthy runs. Find the alarm probability and the fault probability after an alarm.

Review if needed: this section and weighted expectations.

Show hint
Imagine $1000$ runs. Separate true alarms from false alarms before dividing.
Show worked solution

Write $F$ for a fault and $A$ for an alarm. The supplied rates are $\mathbb P(F)=0.1$, $\mathbb P(A\mid F)=0.8$ and $\mathbb P(A\mid F^c)=0.2$. Count hypothetical runs to keep the different denominators visible:

Among 1000 runsAlarmNo alarmTotal
Fault8020100
No fault180720900
Total2607401000

The faulty alarm count is $0.8(100)=80$; the healthy alarm count is $0.2(900)=180$. These are disjoint routes into an alarm, so total probability gives

$$\mathbb P(A)=0.8(0.1)+0.2(0.9)=0.08+0.18=0.26.$$

After an alarm, the reference group is the $260$ alarming runs. Only $80$ of them are faulty:

$$\mathbb P(F\mid A)=\frac{\mathbb P(F\cap A)}{\mathbb P(A)} =\frac{0.08}{0.26}=\frac{80}{260}=\frac4{13}\approx0.3077.$$

The sensitivity $0.8$ is the alarm fraction among faulty runs, not the fault fraction among alarming runs. The large healthy population accounts for the difference. These counts illustrate the assumed law; they are not a new observed data set.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S6 — Hard: Separate noise from disagreement

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S6 — Hard: Separate noise from disagreement

Choose a model label $L\in\{1,2\}$ with equal probabilities. Conditional on $L=1$, $X$ has mean $0$ and variance $1$; conditional on $L=2$, it has mean $4$ and variance $1$. Find the unconditional mean and variance without assuming either conditional law is Gaussian.

Review if needed: this section and weighted expectations.

Show hint
Total variance is average within-model variance plus variance of the model means.
Show worked solution

The model label has probabilities $\mathbb P(L=1)=\mathbb P(L=2)=1/2$. Averaging the conditional means gives the unconditional mean:

$$m=\mathbb E[X]=\frac12\mathbb E[X\mid L=1]+\frac12\mathbb E[X\mid L=2] =\frac12(0)+\frac12(4)=2.$$

Total variance separates spread within each model from disagreement between the model means. The first term is $\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid L)]=(1+1)/2=1$. The conditional mean $m_L$ takes values $0$ and $4$, so

$$\operatorname{Var}(m_L)=\frac12(0-2)^2+\frac12(4-2)^2 =\frac12(4)+\frac12(4)=4.$$

To see why these terms add, write $X-m=(X-m_L)+(m_L-m)$ and expand the square. The cross term has expectation zero: conditional on $L$, the first factor $X-m_L$ has mean zero and the second is fixed. Thus $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1+4=5$.

A second-moment check gives the same result. The conditional second moments are $1+0^2=1$ and $1+4^2=17$, so $\mathbb E[X^2]=(1+17)/2=9$ and $9-m^2=9-4=5$. Neither argument needs Gaussian conditional laws; the supplied finite means and variances suffice.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S7 — Easy: Advance a distribution one step

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S7 — Easy: Advance a distribution one step

A chain has states $A,B$ and row-stochastic transition matrix $P=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.2\\0.3&0.7\end{bmatrix}$. Start in $A$ with certainty. Find the distributions after one and two steps.

Review if needed: this section and matrix-vector multiplication.

Show hint
Use a row distribution $p_t$ and $p_{t+1}=p_tP$.
Show worked solution

Use row distributions because each row of $P$ lists the next-state probabilities from the corresponding current state. Starting certainly in $A$ means $p_0=(1,0)$, so

$$p_1=p_0P=(1,0)\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.2\\0.3&0.7\end{bmatrix}=(0.8,0.2).$$

For the next step, multiply this distribution by $P$ again. Each coordinate adds the two disjoint possible intermediate states:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbb P(s_2=A)&=0.8(0.8)+0.2(0.3)=0.64+0.06=0.70,\\ \mathbb P(s_2=B)&=0.8(0.2)+0.2(0.7)=0.16+0.14=0.30. \end{aligned}$$

Hence $p_2=(0.7,0.3)$, whose coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one. The products use conditional transition probabilities along each path, followed by addition across paths; they do not assume that consecutive states are independent.

Each coordinate adds the two disjoint possible intermediate states: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbb P(s_2=A)&=0.8(0.8)+0.2(0.3)=0.64+0.06=0.70,\\ \mathbb P(s_2=B)&=0.8(0.2)+0.2(0.7)=0.16+0.14=0.30. \end{aligned}$$ Hence $p_2=(0.7,0.3)$, whose coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one. The products use conditional transition probabilities along each path, followed by addition across paths; they do not assume that consecutive states are independent.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S8 — Medium: Solve a stationary distribution

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S8 — Medium: Solve a stationary distribution

For the same $P$, solve $p_*P=p_*$ with $p_*=(a,1-a)$. Does stationarity mean that the chain stops moving?

Review if needed: this section and matrix-vector multiplication.

Show hint
Write only the first coordinate equation, then use the normalisation.
Show worked solution

A stationary distribution is unchanged by one transition. Write $p_*=(a,1-a)$ so its entries already sum to one. The first coordinate of $p_*P=p_*$ gives

$$a=0.8a+0.3(1-a)=0.8a+0.3-0.3a=0.5a+0.3.$$

Subtract $0.5a$ from both sides: $0.5a=0.3$, hence $a=0.3/0.5=0.6$ and $1-a=0.4$. Both are valid probabilities. Check the second coordinate directly:

$$0.6(0.2)+0.4(0.7)=0.12+0.28=0.4.$$

Therefore $p_*=(0.6,0.4)$. Stationarity is a claim about the distribution across possible trajectories. It does not freeze an individual trajectory: whenever it is in $A$, the next state is still $B$ with probability $0.2$, and whenever it is in $B$, it can move to $A$ with probability $0.3$.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S9 — Hard: Why copying data does not increase sample size

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S9 — Hard: Why copying data does not increase sample size

Let $Z_1,\dots,Z_{100}$ be independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $0.2$. Compare the variance of their average with an average of $100$ recorded entries formed by repeating each of $50$ independent Bernoulli draws twice. Both averages are unbiased; are they equally precise?

Review if needed: this section and matrix-vector multiplication.

Show hint
The repeated-data average simplifies to an average of only $50$ independent variables.
Show worked solution

A Bernoulli variable with $p=0.2$ has mean $0.2$ and variance $p(1-p)=0.2(0.8)=0.16$. For $100$ independent draws, the covariances between different draws are zero, so

$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1{100}\sum_{i=1}^{100}Z_i\right) =\frac1{100^2}\sum_{i=1}^{100}\operatorname{Var}(Z_i) =\frac{100(0.16)}{100^2}=0.0016.$$

Let the $50$ genuinely independent draws in the second experiment be $W_1,\ldots,W_{50}$. Repeating each twice changes the recorded list, but its average simplifies:

$$\frac{W_1+W_1+\cdots+W_{50}+W_{50}}{100} =\frac2{100}\sum_{i=1}^{50}W_i=\frac1{50}\sum_{i=1}^{50}W_i.$$

Its variance is therefore $50(0.16)/50^2=0.0032$. Both averages have expectation $0.2$, but their standard deviations are $\sqrt{0.0016}=0.04$ and $\sqrt{0.0032}\approx0.05657$. The second variance is twice as large. Copies of the same draw are perfectly dependent; the independent sample sizes are $100$ and $50$, not $100$ in both cases.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S10 — Easy: Variance is not standard deviation

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S10 — Easy: Variance is not standard deviation

Let $X\sim\mathcal N(10,4)$. Find $\mathbb P(X\le12)$ and $\mathbb P(8\le X\le12)$ using $\Phi(1)\approx0.8413$.

Review if needed: this section and block matrices and Schur complements.

Show hint
In $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ the second number is the variance. Here $\sigma=2$.
Show worked solution

In $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, the second parameter is the variance. Here $\mu=10$, $\sigma^2=4$ and $\sigma=\sqrt4=2$. The standardized variable $Z=(X-10)/2$ has law $\mathcal N(0,1)$.

Because we divide by the positive number $2$, the inequality keeps its direction:

$$X\le12\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{X-10}{2}\le\frac{12-10}{2}=1.$$

Thus $\mathbb P(X\le12)=\Phi(1)\approx0.8413$. For the interval, standardize both endpoints: $(8-10)/2=-1$ and $(12-10)/2=1$. Gaussian symmetry gives $\Phi(-1)=1-\Phi(1)$, so

$$\mathbb P(8\le X\le12)=\Phi(1)-\Phi(-1) =2\Phi(1)-1\approx2(0.8413)-1=0.6826.$$

The interval is one standard deviation on either side of the mean. Its coverage is about $68.3\%$, not $95\%$.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S11 — Medium: One noisy measurement

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S11 — Medium: One noisy measurement

A scalar $f$ has prior $\mathcal N(0,4)$. Observe $y=f+\varepsilon=3$, where $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ is independent of $f$. Find the posterior mean and variance, and the variance of a future noisy measurement with independent noise variance $1$.

Review if needed: this section and block matrices and Schur complements.

Show hint
Add precisions: posterior precision is $1/4+1$. Latent and observation uncertainty differ.
Show worked solution

The independent Gaussian prior and measurement likelihood multiply. Their quadratic terms determine the posterior. With the observed $y=3$, ignore factors constant in $f$ and write the density as proportional to

$$\exp\!\left[-\frac12\left(\frac{f^2}{4}+(3-f)^2\right)\right].$$

Expand and complete the square:

$$\frac{f^2}{4}+(3-f)^2 =\frac54f^2-6f+9 =\frac54\left(f-\frac{12}5\right)^2+\frac95.$$

The constant $9/5$ changes only normalization. A Gaussian exponent has the form $(f-m)^2/s^2$, so the posterior mean is $m=12/5=2.4$ and its variance is $s^2=(5/4)^{-1}=4/5=0.8$. Equivalently, prior precision $1/4$ plus measurement precision $1$ gives $5/4$, and the mean is $(0/4+3)/(5/4)$.

A future reading is $f+\varepsilon_{\rm new}$, where the new noise has variance $1$ and is independent of the posterior offset uncertainty. Conditional on the existing observation, its variance is $4/5+1=9/5=1.8$. The mean remains $2.4$. The latent variance $0.8$ answers uncertainty about $f$; the larger predictive variance answers uncertainty about a new noisy reading.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S12 — Hard: A chance constraint along a direction

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S12 — Hard: A chance constraint along a direction

Let $X$ be jointly Gaussian with mean $(1,2)$ and covariance $\begin{bmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&4\end{bmatrix}$. For $S=X_1+X_2$, compute its mean and variance. Find the smallest $b$ satisfying $\mathbb P(S\le b)\ge0.95$, using $\Phi^{-1}(0.95)\approx1.64485$.

Review if needed: this section and block matrices and Schur complements.

Show hint
Use $S=h^\top X$ with $h=(1,1)$. Include both cross-covariance terms.
Show worked solution

A linear combination of a jointly Gaussian vector is Gaussian. For $S=h^\top X$ with $h=(1,1)^\top$, the mean is $h^\top(1,2)^\top=1+2=3$. The variance includes both off-diagonal covariance contributions:

$$\operatorname{Var}(S)=h^\top\Sigma h =1(1)1+1(0.5)1+1(0.5)1+1(4)1=6.$$

Thus $S\sim\mathcal N(3,6)$ and its standard deviation is $\sqrt6$. Standardization converts the requirement to

$$\mathbb P(S\le b)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{b-3}{\sqrt6}\right)\ge0.95.$$

Since $\Phi$ is strictly increasing, this holds exactly when $(b-3)/\sqrt6\ge\Phi^{-1}(0.95)$. Multiplying by the positive $\sqrt6$ and adding $3$ gives the smallest threshold

$$b_* = 3+\sqrt6\,\Phi^{-1}(0.95)\approx7.0291.$$

The supplied rounded quantile instead gives $3+1.64485\sqrt6\approx7.0290$. exercises.label: Exercise C.S13 — Easy: An upper bound can be loose

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S13 — Easy: An upper bound can be loose

A nonnegative random cost $X$ has mean $2$. Bound $\mathbb P(X\ge8)$ with Markov's inequality. What does the same method say about $\mathbb P(X\ge1)$?

Review if needed: this section and logarithms and rates.

Show hint
A probability cannot exceed one, even when an inequality returns a larger number.
Show worked solution

Markov's inequality applies to a nonnegative random variable. One way to see the bound is that on the event $A=\{X\ge8\}$, the cost is at least $8$, while outside it the cost is still nonnegative. Therefore $\mathbb E[X]\ge8\mathbb P(A)$, and

$$\mathbb P(X\ge8)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}8=\frac28=\frac14.$$

At the threshold $1$, the same argument yields $\mathbb P(X\ge1)\le2/1=2$. This remains a true inequality, but every probability also satisfies $\mathbb P(X\ge1)\le1$. Combining the two bounds gives $\mathbb P(X\ge1)\le\min(2,1)=1$.

The first calculation gives a useful upper limit; the second gives no restriction beyond the definition of probability. Neither is an estimate of the actual tail probability from a specified distribution.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S14 — Medium: Plan a Hoeffding sample size

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S14 — Medium: Plan a Hoeffding sample size

Independent observations lie in $[0,1]$ and have a common mean $\mu$. How many observations suffice to bound $|\bar X_N-\mu|$ by $0.1$ with confidence at least $0.95$ using Hoeffding?

Review if needed: this section and logarithms and rates.

Show hint
Solve $2e^{-2N(0.1)^2}\le0.05$ and round upward.
Show worked solution

The observations are independent, bounded in $[0,1]$ and have the common mean $\mu$, so two-sided Hoeffding gives

$$\mathbb P(|\bar X_N-\mu|\ge0.1)\le 2\exp[-2N(0.1)^2]=2e^{-0.02N}.$$

To make this failure bound at most $0.05$, solve the inequality rather than round a guessed sample size:

$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{-0.02N}&\le0.05,\\ e^{-0.02N}&\le0.025=\frac1{40},\\ -0.02N&\le-\ln40,\\ N&\ge\frac{\ln40}{0.02}\approx184.44397. \end{aligned}$$

The logarithm preserves the inequality because it is increasing on positive numbers; division by $-0.02$ reverses it. Since $N$ must be an integer, choose $N=185$. The bounds at $184$ and $185$ are approximately $0.05045$ and $0.04945$, confirming the rounding direction.

This is the smallest integer certified by this Hoeffding calculation. It does not assert that no smaller sample could work for a more specifically known law.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S15 — Hard: A bounded bias survives averaging

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S15 — Hard: A bounded bias survives averaging

Let independent errors be uniform on $[0,2]$. A learner treats them as zero-mean noise and chooses $R=2$. Explain why the zero-mean sub-Gaussian condition fails. Centre the errors correctly and give a valid Hoeffding sub-Gaussian parameter for the centred errors.

Review if needed: this section and logarithms and rates.

Show hint
First compute the expectation. The centred interval has length $2$, and Hoeffding uses half that length.
Show worked solution

A uniform error on $[0,2]$ has mean $(0+2)/2=1$. Independence makes averaging reduce its random fluctuations, but it does not remove that mean: the average tends to $1$, not $0$.

The zero-mean sub-Gaussian condition asks for $\mathbb E[e^{\lambda\varepsilon}]\le e^{\lambda^2R^2/2}$ for every real $\lambda$. For the claimed $R=2$, there is a concrete contradiction. At $\lambda=1/4$, integrate the uniform density:

$$\mathbb E[e^{\varepsilon/4}] =\frac12\int_0^2e^{x/4}\,dx =2(e^{1/2}-1)\approx1.29744,$$

whereas the proposed upper bound is $e^{(1/4)^2(2)^2/2}=e^{1/8}\approx1.13315$. The left side is larger. More generally, a nonzero mean produces a linear term $1+\lambda\mathbb E[\varepsilon]+O(\lambda^2)$ near zero, while the claimed bound has no linear term.

Center correctly with $\xi=\varepsilon-1$. Then $\mathbb E[\xi]=1-1=0$ and $\xi\in[-1,1]$. Hoeffding's lemma for a centered variable in $[a,b]$ gives $R=(b-a)/2$, hence $R=(1-(-1))/2=1$ here. The observation model becomes $y=f+1+\xi$: the bias $1$ must be included or corrected separately.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S16 — Easy: One statement or all statements?

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S16 — Easy: One statement or all statements?

Three safety checks each fail with probability at most $0.01$. Give a lower bound on the probability that all three pass. Must the failures be independent?

Review if needed: this section and unions and quantifiers.

Show hint
The complement of all passing is the union of the failure events.
Show worked solution

Let $F_i$ be the event that check $i$ fails. All three pass exactly on $(F_1\cup F_2\cup F_3)^c$: the complement of at least one failure.

The union bound follows because counting the probabilities separately can count outcomes that fail several checks more than once. It therefore gives an upper bound:

$$\mathbb P(F_1\cup F_2\cup F_3) \le\mathbb P(F_1)+\mathbb P(F_2)+\mathbb P(F_3) \le0.01+0.01+0.01=0.03.$$

Taking a complement yields $\mathbb P(\text{all pass})=1-\mathbb P(\text{any failure})\ge1-0.03=0.97$.

No independence is needed. If passing events were independent, their probabilities could instead be multiplied, giving at least $0.99^3=0.970299$. That stronger bound uses an extra assumption; the supplied marginal bounds alone justify $0.97$.

solution.html:
Let $F_i$ be the event that check $i$ fails. All three pass exactly on $(F_1\cup F_2\cup F_3)^c$: the complement of at least one failure.

The union bound follows because counting the probabilities separately can count outcomes that fail several checks more than once. It therefore gives an upper bound:

$$\mathbb P(F_1\cup F_2\cup F_3) \le\mathbb P(F_1)+\mathbb P(F_2)+\mathbb P(F_3) \le0.01+0.01+0.01=0.03.$$

Taking a complement yields $\mathbb P(\text{all pass})=1-\mathbb P(\text{any failure})\ge1-0.03=0.97$.

No independence is needed. If passing events were independent, their probabilities could instead be multiplied, giving at least $0.99^3=0.970299$. That stronger bound uses an extra assumption; the supplied marginal bounds alone justify $0.97$.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S17 — Medium: A finite grid of confidence intervals

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S17 — Medium: A finite grid of confidence intervals

You want simultaneous confidence $0.95$ for $10$ sample means. Each uses $N$ independent observations in $[0,1]$ with a common mean $\mu_i$ within that data set, and must estimate its $\mu_i$ with absolute error at most $0.1$. Assign equal failure budgets and find a sufficient common $N$. The ten data sets may depend on one another.

Review if needed: this section and unions and quantifiers.

Show hint
Give each mean budget $0.05/10$, then apply two-sided Hoeffding within that data set.
Show worked solution

Let $F_i=\{|\bar X_{i,N}-\mu_i|\ge0.1\}$ for the ten means. A total failure budget $0.05$ shared equally gives $\delta_i=0.05/10=0.005$. Within each data set, its own independent observations lie in $[0,1]$, so Hoeffding applies:

$$\mathbb P(F_i)\le2e^{-2N(0.1)^2}=2e^{-0.02N}.$$

Impose this bound separately for every $i$ and solve:

$$2e^{-0.02N}\le0.005 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ e^{-0.02N}\le0.0025=\frac1{400} \ \Longleftrightarrow\ N\ge\frac{\ln400}{0.02}\approx299.5732.$$

Round upward to $N=300$ observations per mean. The probability that at least one mean misses its target is then at most $\sum_{i=1}^{10}\delta_i=10(0.005)=0.05$, so all ten targets hold together with probability at least $0.95$.

Independence is used within each data set for Hoeffding, and not between data sets for the union bound. Giving each mean a pointwise failure budget $0.05$ would instead sum to $0.5$, providing only the lower bound $1-0.5=0.5$ for simultaneous success.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S18 — Hard: Guarantees at every time

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S18 — Hard: Guarantees at every time

For times $t=1,2,\dots$, assign failure budgets $\delta_t=0.05/[t(t+1)]$. Prove that all time-indexed statements hold together with probability at least $0.95$, provided each has failure probability at most $\delta_t$. Can you instead assign $0.05$ at every time?

Review if needed: this section and unions and quantifiers.

Show hint
Use $1/[t(t+1)]=1/t-1/(t+1)$ and take the limit of its partial sums.
Show worked solution

Write $F_t$ for failure at time $t$. For any finite $T$, the union bound and the supplied individual guarantees give $\mathbb P(\bigcup_{t=1}^T F_t)\le\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_t$. The reciprocal identity in the hint makes the sum explicit:

$$\begin{aligned} \sum_{t=1}^T\delta_t &=0.05\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\frac1t-\frac1{t+1}\right)\\ &=0.05\left[(1-\tfrac12)+(\tfrac12-\tfrac13)+\cdots+ (\tfrac1T-\tfrac1{T+1})\right]\\ &=0.05\left(1-\frac1{T+1}\right). \end{aligned}$$

The intermediate terms cancel. Letting $T$ grow gives total budget $0.05$. The finite unions increase to the event of any failure at any positive time, so the countable union bound gives $\mathbb P(\bigcup_{t=1}^\infty F_t)\le0.05$. Its complement, all statements holding at all times, has probability at least $0.95$.

A budget $0.05$ at every time does not justify the same conclusion: the sum through $T$ would be $0.05T$ and the infinite sum diverges. To see that this is a real gap, choose independent failures each of probability $0.05$. Then no failure through $T$ has probability $0.95^T\to0$, so an eventual failure has probability one. Independence is needed for that counterexample, not for the summable-budget guarantee.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S19 — Easy: A fair random walk

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S19 — Easy: A fair random walk

Let $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\dots$ be independent fair signs, taking $-1$ and $1$ with equal probability. Put $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^t\varepsilon_i$, with $S_0=0$. What is $\mathbb E[S_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]$, where $\mathcal F_t$ records the first $t$ signs?

Review if needed: this section and conditional expectation.

Show hint
At time $t$, $S_t$ is known and the next independent sign still has mean zero.
Show worked solution

Separate the already recorded sum from the next increment:

$$S_{t+1}=S_t+\varepsilon_{t+1}.$$

At time $t$, the information $\mathcal F_t$ determines $S_t$, so conditioning leaves it unchanged. The next sign is independent of that past and still equally likely to be $-1$ or $1$; its conditional mean is $(-1)(1/2)+1(1/2)=0$. Hence

$$\mathbb E[S_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t] =S_t+\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t] =S_t+0=S_t.$$

Each $S_t$ is measurable from the first $t$ signs and integrable because $|S_t|\le t$. Together with the displayed conditional equality, these are the martingale conditions. A martingale need not remain constant: this walk changes by one on every step, while its expected next change given the past is zero.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S20 — Medium: An adaptive multiplier can preserve zero drift

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S20 — Medium: An adaptive multiplier can preserve zero drift

Before seeing a fair sign $\varepsilon_t$, choose $a_t=2$ if the current random-walk sum $S_{t-1}\ge0$, and $a_t=1$ otherwise. Define $D_t=a_t\varepsilon_t$. Show that $\mathbb E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0$ and find a valid conditional sub-Gaussian parameter.

Review if needed: this section and conditional expectation.

Show hint
The multiplier is already known when conditioning on the past; its magnitude never exceeds $2$.
Show worked solution

The choice $a_t$ uses only $S_{t-1}$, so it is known from $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ before the new sign arrives. This is the predictability needed to take it outside the conditional expectation. Since the next fair sign has conditional mean zero,

$$\mathbb E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] =\mathbb E[a_t\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] =a_t\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] =a_t(0)=0.$$

Given that past, $a_t$ is a fixed positive number, either $1$ or $2$, and $D_t$ takes values $-a_t,a_t$ with equal probabilities. Its conditional law is centered and supported in an interval of length $2a_t$. Conditional Hoeffding's lemma therefore gives

$$\mathbb E[e^{\lambda D_t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] \le e^{\lambda^2a_t^2/2}\le e^{\lambda^2(2)^2/2}\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb R).$$

The second inequality uses $a_t\le2$. Thus $a_t$ is a valid conditional parameter for that particular past, and the fixed choice $R=2$ works uniformly at every time. Adaptation can create dependence between increments; the argument uses predictable choices and a centered conditional law instead of independence of the $D_t$.

solution.html:
The choice $a_t$ uses only $S_{t-1}$, so it is known from $\mathcal F_{t-1}$ before the new sign arrives. This is the predictability needed to take it outside the conditional expectation. Since the next fair sign has conditional mean zero,

$$\mathbb E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] =\mathbb E[a_t\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] =a_t\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] =a_t(0)=0.$$

Given that past, $a_t$ is a fixed positive number, either $1$ or $2$, and $D_t$ takes values $-a_t,a_t$ with equal probabilities. Its conditional law is centered and supported in an interval of length $2a_t$. Conditional Hoeffding's lemma therefore gives

$$\mathbb E[e^{\lambda D_t}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}] \le e^{\lambda^2a_t^2/2}\le e^{\lambda^2(2)^2/2}\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb R).$$

The second inequality uses $a_t\le2$. Thus $a_t$ is a valid conditional parameter for that particular past, and the fixed choice $R=2$ works uniformly at every time. Adaptation can create dependence between increments; the argument uses predictable choices and a centered conditional law instead of independence of the $D_t$.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S21 — Hard: Looking ahead breaks the argument

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S21 — Hard: Looking ahead breaks the argument

A learner first observes a fair sign $\varepsilon_t$ and then chooses $a_t=\varepsilon_t$. It claims that $D_t=a_t\varepsilon_t$ has mean zero because the original noise is fair. Compute its conditional mean and identify the failed step.

Review if needed: this section and conditional expectation.

Show hint
List the two possible sign values and square them.
Show worked solution

List both possible outcomes of the new sign. If $\varepsilon_t=1$, then $a_t=1$ and $D_t=1\cdot1=1$. If $\varepsilon_t=-1$, then $a_t=-1$ and $D_t=(-1)(-1)=1$. Thus $D_t=\varepsilon_t^2=1$ for every outcome.

A constant remains that constant after conditioning:

$$\mathbb E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\mathbb E[1\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=1.$$

Its accumulated sum after $T$ steps is $T$, so it has positive deterministic drift. The failed step would be to write $\mathbb E[a_t\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=a_t\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]$. That requires $a_t$ to be determined by the past, but here it depends on the new sign itself.

Fairness gives mean zero for $\varepsilon_t$, not for every data-dependent transformation of it. In particular, the product of these dependent factors has mean $1$ even though each factor individually has mean zero.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S22 — Easy: Entropy of a fair and a biased coin

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S22 — Easy: Entropy of a fair and a biased coin

Using natural logarithms, compute the entropy of a fair Bernoulli variable and a Bernoulli variable with success probability $1/4$. Use $H(p)=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p)$.

Review if needed: this section and discrete probability laws.

Show hint
Both outcomes contribute, even if you call one of them a failure.
Show worked solution

Entropy averages the negative logarithm of an outcome's probability over both outcomes. For a fair coin, use $\ln(1/2)=-\ln2$:

$$H(1/2)=-\frac12\ln\frac12-\frac12\ln\frac12 =\frac12\ln2+\frac12\ln2=\ln2\approx0.693147\text{ nats}.$$

For success probability $1/4$, the failure probability is $3/4$, not zero. Substitute both probabilities:

$$\begin{aligned} H(1/4)&=-\frac14\ln\frac14-\frac34\ln\frac34\\ &\approx-\frac14(-1.386294)-\frac34(-0.287682)\\ &\approx0.346574+0.215762=0.562335\text{ nats}. \end{aligned}$$

The biased coin has lower entropy: knowing its bias makes its result more predictable. Natural logarithms give nats; using base-two logarithms would give bits. The numerical values above are rounded evaluations of the exact expressions.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S23 — Medium: Total variation and directional KL

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S23 — Medium: Total variation and directional KL

For $p=(0.75,0.25)$ and $q=(0.5,0.5)$, compute $\operatorname{TV}(p,q)$, $D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)$ and $D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)$.

Review if needed: this section and discrete probability laws.

Show hint
TV is half the sum of absolute probability differences. In KL, the first distribution supplies the averaging weights.
Show worked solution

Both laws put positive mass on each outcome, so both KL directions are finite. Total variation compares coordinate differences symmetrically:

$$\operatorname{TV}(p,q)=\frac12\left(|0.75-0.5|+|0.25-0.5|\right) =\frac12(0.25+0.25)=0.25.$$

For KL, use the first law as the averaging weights and form its ratios to the second law:

$$\begin{aligned} D_{\rm KL}(p\|q) &=0.75\ln\frac{0.75}{0.5}+0.25\ln\frac{0.25}{0.5}\\ &=0.75\ln1.5+0.25\ln0.5\\ &\approx0.304099-0.173287=0.130812\text{ nats}. \end{aligned}$$

Reversing direction changes both ratios and weights:

$$D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)=0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.75}+0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.25} =0.5\ln\frac23+0.5\ln2 \approx-0.202733+0.346574=0.143841.$$

The two KL values differ, while TV is unchanged on reversal. This direction dependence is one reason KL is not a distance metric.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S24 — Hard: Support mismatch and a useless KL bound

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S24 — Hard: Support mismatch and a useless KL bound

Let $p=(1,0)$ and $q=(0.5,0.5)$. Compute both KL directions and TV, using the convention $0\ln(0/q)=0$. Apply Pinsker to the finite KL direction.

Review if needed: this section and discrete probability laws.

Show hint
Positive mass in the first law where the second law is zero makes that KL infinite.
Show worked solution

For $D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)$, the first outcome contributes $1\ln(1/0.5)=\ln2$. The second outcome has zero $p$-mass and contributes zero by the stated convention. Therefore

$$D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)=\ln2\approx0.693147.$$

In the reverse direction, $q$ assigns positive mass $0.5$ to the second outcome but $p$ assigns zero. Its logarithmic ratio is infinite, so $D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)=+\infty$. This is a support mismatch, not a large finite rounding error.

Total variation stays finite because it uses absolute probability differences:

$$\operatorname{TV}(p,q)=\frac12(|1-0.5|+|0-0.5|) =\frac12(0.5+0.5)=0.5.$$

Pinsker can use the finite KL direction:

$$0.5=\operatorname{TV}(p,q)\le \sqrt{\frac{D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)}2}=\sqrt{\frac{\ln2}2}\approx0.588705.$$

This is a valid upper bound but does not reproduce the exact TV. Using the infinite reverse KL would give an infinite upper bound and no useful restriction.

Exercise C.S25 — Easy: Find the first threshold reaching the target

A loss $L$ equals $0$, $10$, $100$ with probabilities $0.8$, $0.15$, $0.05$. Using $\operatorname{VaR}_\alpha(L)=\inf\{z:F_L(z)\ge\alpha\}$, find VaR at levels $0.8$, $0.9$ and $0.95$.

Review if needed: this section and CDFs and atoms.

Show hint
Write the cumulative masses at the three possible loss values. The definition uses $\ge$, not $\gt$.
Show worked solution

First write the CDF, which includes all mass at or below the threshold:

$$F_L(z)= \begin{cases} 0,&z\lt0,\\ 0.8,&0\le z\lt10,\\ 0.95,&10\le z\lt100,\\ 1,&100\le z. \end{cases}$$

At level $0.8$, every threshold below $0$ has CDF zero, while $z=0$ reaches $0.8$. Thus the infimum in the definition is $\operatorname{VaR}_{0.8}(L)=0$.

At level $0.9$, the CDF remains $0.8$ until the jump at $10$, where it becomes $0.8+0.15=0.95$. Hence $\operatorname{VaR}_{0.9}(L)=10$. At level $0.95$, the same threshold already satisfies the non-strict condition $F_L(10)\ge0.95$, giving $\operatorname{VaR}_{0.95}(L)=10$ as well.

The equality case matters at an atom. VaR $10$ at level $0.95$ still leaves the $0.05$ probability of loss $100$ above that threshold; it is not a statement that the loss cannot exceed $10$.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S26 — Medium: Take the worst ten percent, including part of an atom

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S26 — Medium: Take the worst ten percent, including part of an atom

For the same law, compute $\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(L)$ as the average of the worst $10\%$ of probability mass. Compare it with $\mathbb E[L]$ and with $\mathbb E[L\mid L\ge10]$.

Review if needed: this section and CDFs and atoms.

Show hint
Use all $5\%$ mass at $100$ and only $5\%$ of the $15\%$ mass at $10$.
Show worked solution

The worst $10\%$ means selecting probability mass $1-0.9=0.1$ from the highest losses downward. Use all the $0.05$ mass at loss $100$. That leaves $0.1-0.05=0.05$ mass to take from the loss-$10$ atom, which has total mass $0.15$.

Only one third of that atom is needed. Divide the loss-weighted selected mass by the selected mass:

$$\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(L)= \frac{0.05(100)+0.05(10)}{0.1} =\frac{5+0.5}{0.1}=55.$$

The full expectation instead includes every outcome with its original probability:

$$\mathbb E[L]=0.8(0)+0.15(10)+0.05(100)=0+1.5+5=6.5.$$

The event $L\ge10$ contains $0.15+0.05=0.2$ mass. Its conditional mean is

$$\mathbb E[L\mid L\ge10] =\frac{0.15(10)+0.05(100)}{0.2}=\frac{6.5}{0.2}=32.5.$$

This conditions on the worst $20\%$, rather than selecting exactly the worst $10\%$. Atoms at VaR must be split when necessary; using the entire event $L\ge\operatorname{VaR}_{0.9}$ would give the wrong CVaR here.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S27 — Hard: Verify the optimisation formula at a kink

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S27 — Hard: Verify the optimisation formula at a kink

For the same loss, minimise $g(\nu)=\nu+10\mathbb E[(L-\nu)^+]$, where $z^+=\max(z,0)$. Find its slopes on $(-\infty,0)$, $(0,10)$, $(10,100)$ and $(100,\infty)$, and its minimum.

Review if needed: this section and CDFs and atoms.

Show hint
Away from atoms, $g'(\nu)=1-10\mathbb P(L\gt\nu)$. Track how the tail probability jumps.
Show worked solution

Expand the expectation into the three possible losses:

$$g(\nu)=\nu+10\left[0.8(0-\nu)^+ +0.15(10-\nu)^++0.05(100-\nu)^+\right].$$

On each open interval, we know which positive parts are active. Substitute those expressions and simplify:

$$g(\nu)= \begin{cases} \nu+10(6.5-\nu)=65-9\nu,&\nu\lt0,\\ \nu+10(6.5-0.2\nu)=65-\nu,&0\lt\nu\lt10,\\ \nu+10(5-0.05\nu)=50+0.5\nu,&10\lt\nu\lt100,\\ \nu,&100\lt\nu. \end{cases}$$

For example, on $(0,10)$ only losses $10$ and $100$ contribute, giving $0.15(10-\nu)+0.05(100-\nu)=6.5-0.2\nu$. The four slopes are therefore $-9,-1,0.5,1$. The positive-part function is continuous, so these decreasing pieces lead up to $10$ and the increasing pieces start after $10$.

The minimum occurs at that kink. Direct substitution avoids differentiating where the derivative does not exist:

$$\mathbb E[(L-10)^+]=0.8(0)+0.15(0)+0.05(90)=4.5,\qquad g(10)=10+10(4.5)=55.$$

This agrees with the preceding split-tail CVaR. A kink can be a minimizer because the slope changes from negative to positive.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S28 — Easy: Exactly two failures

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S28 — Easy: Exactly two failures

Four independent runs each fail with probability $0.1$. Find the probability of exactly two failures and the probability of at least one failure.

Review if needed: this section and conditional probabilities.

Show hint
For exactly two failures, count the possible pairs. For at least one, take the complement of zero failures.
Show worked solution

For a specified pair of failing runs, independence gives probability $0.1^2(0.9)^2=0.01(0.81)=0.0081$: both selected runs fail and both others pass.

There are $\binom42=4!/(2!2!)=6$ different choices of the pair. Their exact-two-failure events are disjoint, so

$$\mathbb P(\text{exactly two failures})=6(0.0081)=0.0486.$$

For at least one failure, taking a complement is shorter than adding all the possible counts. No failure means that all four runs pass, with probability $0.9^4=0.6561$. Therefore

$$\mathbb P(\text{at least one failure})=1-0.9^4=1-0.6561=0.3439.$$

Independence justifies multiplying run probabilities. Disjointness justifies adding the six patterns; these are two distinct steps in the calculation.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S29 — Medium: Zero failures still leaves uncertainty

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S29 — Medium: Zero failures still leaves uncertainty

Observe zero failures in $100$ independent runs with a fixed unknown failure probability $p$. Find the exact one-sided $95\%$ upper confidence limit by solving $(1-p_U)^{100}=0.05$. Interpret it without assigning a posterior probability to $p$.

Review if needed: this section and conditional probabilities.

Show hint
Take the hundredth root. The confidence statement describes the repeated-data procedure.
Show worked solution

For a fixed failure probability $p$, independence gives probability $(1-p)^{100}$ of seeing zero failures. The one-sided $95\%$ upper limit puts this observed extreme outcome at the boundary probability $0.05$:

$$\begin{aligned} (1-p_U)^{100}&=0.05,\\ 1-p_U&=0.05^{1/100},\\ p_U&=1-0.05^{1/100} =1-\exp\!\left(\frac{\ln0.05}{100}\right) \approx0.029513. \end{aligned}$$

The positive hundredth root is the relevant one because $1-p_U$ is a probability. If a proposed true $p$ were larger than this limit, then $1-p$ would be smaller and observing zero failures would have probability below $0.05$. Inverting these binomial-tail tests gives the upper confidence-limit procedure.

The confidence statement concerns that procedure over repeated random data sets: its reported upper limit covers a fixed true $p$ with probability at least $0.95$. After this particular data set, it is not a posterior probability distribution for $p$. exercises.label: Exercise C.S30 — Hard: Ranks, ties and marginal coverage

exercise.html:
Exercise C.S30 — Hard: Ranks, ties and marginal coverage

There are $19$ calibration scores and one future score. Assume all $20$ scores are jointly exchangeable and distinct almost surely. A prediction rule accepts the future point when its score is at most the $18$th smallest calibration score. Find its marginal acceptance probability. Why need this not be $90\%$ for each subgroup?

Review if needed: this section and conditional probabilities.

Show hint
Among all $20$ scores the future score has a uniform rank. Compare that rank with $18$.
Show worked solution

Let $R$ denote the future score's rank among all $20$ scores, counted from the smallest. With no ties, exactly one score occupies each rank. Exchangeability says the future label is equally likely to be any of those scores, so $\mathbb P(R=r)=1/20$ for every $r=1,\ldots,20$.

Now compare an overall rank with the calibration threshold. If $R\le18$, at most $17$ calibration scores are smaller than the future score, so the $18$th calibration score is above it. If $R\ge19$, at least $18$ calibration scores are smaller, so the future score exceeds that threshold. Thus acceptance is exactly the event $R\le18$:

$$\mathbb P(\text{accept})=\sum_{r=1}^{18}\mathbb P(R=r) =18\left(\frac1{20}\right)=0.9.$$

This probability averages over the random calibration scores and the future point. It does not condition on a particular subgroup or on the calibration set we happened to obtain. To see why an average does not fix subgroup values, two equally common groups with acceptance probabilities $0.8$ and $1$ would give $(0.8+1)/2=0.9$ overall. The same marginal target is compatible with undercoverage in one group.

The no-ties assumption makes the rank equivalence exact; ties would require an additional tie-handling argument rather than automatically reusing this calculation.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B1 — Easy: A new production line changes the inspection decision

exercise.html:
Exercise C.B1 — Easy: A new production line changes the inspection decision

Keep the sensor rates and costs from example 1, but change the incoming fault probability to $0.01$. Should an alarm still trigger inspection? Compare always releasing with retaining the old inspect-on-alarm rule.

Review: conditional probability and Bayes; the inspection decision.

Show hint

Recompute both routes into an alarm, then compare the posterior fault probability with $0.20$.

Show worked solution

Keep $F$ for a fault and $A$ for an alarm. The new base rate is $\mathbb P(F)=0.01$, while the sensor still has $\mathbb P(A\mid F)=0.90$ and $\mathbb P(A\mid F^c)=0.08$. Compute the two disjoint alarm routes:

$$\mathbb P(F\cap A)=0.01(0.90)=0.009,\qquad \mathbb P(F^c\cap A)=0.99(0.08)=0.0792.$$

Therefore $\mathbb P(A)=0.009+0.0792=0.0882$ and

$$\mathbb P(F\mid A)=\frac{0.009}{0.0882} =\frac{90}{882}=\frac5{49}\approx0.10204.$$

Inspection costs $6$ units and release after information $I$ costs $30\mathbb P(F\mid I)$. After an alarm, release costs $30(5/49)=150/49\approx3.0612$, below $6$, so an alarm should no longer trigger inspection in this expected-cost model.

Check silence as well. Missed faults have probability $0.01(0.10)=0.001$, and silence has probability $1-0.0882=0.9118$. Thus $\mathbb P(F\mid A^c)=0.001/0.9118\approx0.001097$, also below the inspection threshold $6/30=0.20$. Release is preferred in both information states.

Always releasing costs $30(0.01)=0.30$ units per package. Keeping the old inspect-on-alarm rule costs $6(0.0882)+30(0.001)=0.5292+0.03=0.5592$: inspection cost on alarms plus jam cost on missed faults. The unchanged rule is more expensive after the base-rate change. This comparison relies on the stated costs and perfect-inspection model; it does not promise that every released package is sound.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B2 — Medium: Offset uncertainty is not reading uncertainty

exercise.html:
Exercise C.B2 — Medium: Offset uncertainty is not reading uncertainty

After example 2, a new measurement has zero-mean Gaussian noise $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1\ \mathrm{mm}^2)$, independent of the offset and calibration noises. After subtracting the posterior mean offset, what is the probability that its total error lies within $2$ mm? Does the $0.98$ requirement hold for this new quantity?

Review: Gaussian conditioning and standardisation; the calibration model.

Show hint

The total error is $\theta-m+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{new}}$. Add the variances of these independent Gaussian terms conditional on the calibration data.

Show worked solution

Condition on the two calibration readings from example 2. Their posterior is $\theta\mid\text{data}\sim\mathcal N(m,s^2)$ with $m=7/6$ mm and $s^2=2/3\ {\rm mm}^2$. Subtracting $m$ centers the residual offset: $\theta-m$ has mean zero and variance $2/3$.

A corrected new reading has total error $e=\theta-m+\varepsilon_{\rm new}$. The fresh noise is independent of the offset and calibration data, so these two terms remain independent conditional on those data. A sum of independent Gaussian terms is Gaussian, with

$$\mathbb E[e\mid\text{data}]=0+0=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(e\mid\text{data})=\frac23+1=\frac53\ {\rm mm}^2.$$

The predictive standard deviation is $\sqrt{5/3}\approx1.2910$ mm. Standardize both sides of the tolerance interval:

$$\mathbb P(|e|\le2\mid\text{data}) =\mathbb P\!\left(-\frac2{\sqrt{5/3}}\le Z\le\frac2{\sqrt{5/3}}\right) =2\Phi\!\left(\frac2{\sqrt{5/3}}\right)-1\approx0.87866,$$

where $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and the standardized upper endpoint is about $1.54919$. This is below $0.98$. The earlier probability $0.98569$ concerned only $\theta-m$, not a new noisy measurement. Mean correction removes the systematic center, while posterior offset uncertainty and fresh measurement noise still contribute spread.

Standardize both sides of the tolerance interval: $$\mathbb P(|e|\le2\mid\text{data}) =\mathbb P\!\left(-\frac2{\sqrt{5/3}}\le Z\le\frac2{\sqrt{5/3}}\right) =2\Phi\!\left(\frac2{\sqrt{5/3}}\right)-1\approx0.87866,$$ where $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and the standardized upper endpoint is about $1.54919$. This is below $0.98$. The earlier probability $0.98569$ concerned only $\theta-m$, not a new noisy measurement. Mean correction removes the systematic center, while posterior offset uncertainty and fresh measurement noise still contribute spread.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B3 — Hard: Repeated use shares the same uncertain offset

exercise.html:
Exercise C.B3 — Hard: Repeated use shares the same uncertain offset

Average $100$ new corrected readings of the same fixed displacement after example 2. Their zero-mean noises are mutually independent and independent of the offset and calibration noises, each with variance $1\ \mathrm{mm}^2$. Find the average's error variance and its limiting value as the number of readings grows. Explain why the variance is not $(5/3)/100$.

Review: variance and covariance; shared offset uncertainty.

Show hint

Write the average error as one shared offset error plus an average of fresh noises. Only the second term is averaged away.

Show worked solution

Keep the correction $m$ determined by the existing calibration data, and condition on those data. Put $U=\theta-m$, so $\operatorname{Var}(U)=2/3\ {\rm mm}^2$. Reading $i$ has error $e_i=U+\varepsilon_i$: the same $U$ occurs in every reading.

Averaging $n$ readings gives

$$\bar e_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(U+\varepsilon_i) =\frac{nU}{n}+\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i =U+\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i.$$

The new noises are mutually independent, independent of $U$, and each have variance $1$. Thus their average has variance $n/n^2=1/n$ and zero covariance with $U$:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar e_n)=\frac23+\frac1n,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\bar e_{100})=\frac23+\frac1{100} =\frac{200+3}{300}=\frac{203}{300}\approx0.67667\ {\rm mm}^2.$$

As $n\to\infty$, $1/n\to0$, leaving variance $2/3$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{2/3}\approx0.8165$ mm. More repeated readings reduce fresh noise, but the common offset does not average away.

For $i\ne j$, independence of the fresh noises gives $\operatorname{Cov}(e_i,e_j)=\operatorname{Var}(U)=2/3$. The usual division of a single reading's variance $5/3$ by $n$ would discard those cross-covariances. Reducing this floor requires improved calibration of the shared offset, rather than treating copies of the same offset uncertainty as independent.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B4 — Hard: Plan a batch reliability requirement

exercise.html:
Exercise C.B4 — Hard: Plan a batch reliability requirement

A revised inspection process has an assumed per-package escape probability $q$. Require the probability of any escaped fault in a batch of $50$ packages to be at most $0.02$. Find a sufficient bound on $q$ without independence. If escapes are independent with equal probability, find the exact largest $q$. Does example 1's $q=0.004$ meet either bound?

Review: union bounds and simultaneous events; the escape probability.

Show hint

Use a union bound first. Under independence, compute the probability that all $50$ packages avoid an escape.

Show worked solution

Let $E_i$ denote an escaped fault on package $i$, with $\mathbb P(E_i)=q$. Any escaped fault in the batch is the union $\bigcup_{i=1}^{50}E_i$. Without an independence assumption, the union bound gives

$$\mathbb P(\text{any escape})\le\sum_{i=1}^{50}\mathbb P(E_i)=50q.$$

It is sufficient to require $50q\le0.02$, or $q\le0.02/50=0.0004$. This is a sufficient allowance valid under arbitrary dependence.

With independent escapes of equal probability, no escape has exact probability $(1-q)^{50}$. Solve the exact batch requirement:

$$\begin{aligned} 1-(1-q)^{50}&\le0.02,\\ (1-q)^{50}&\ge0.98,\\ 1-q&\ge0.98^{1/50},\\ q&\le1-0.98^{1/50}\approx0.000403973. \end{aligned}$$

The positive root preserves order on $[0,1]$. The exact independent allowance is slightly larger because the union bound can overcount outcomes with several escapes.

Example 1's $q=0.004$ exceeds both allowances. The union bound would only certify the much larger bound $50(0.004)=0.20$; under independence, the actual batch probability is $1-0.996^{50}\approx0.18160$, above $0.02$. These calculations start from assumed per-package rates. They are not statistical confidence limits inferred from observing a batch.

exercises.label: Exercise C.1 — Monte Carlo estimates and zero failures

exercise.html:
Exercise C.1 — Monte Carlo estimates and zero failures

In $200$ independent simulated episodes, $14$ contain at least one violation. (a) Estimate the violation probability and its standard error. (b) Give the normal-approximation 95% interval. (c) Now suppose $0$ of $200$ episodes violate. What does the standard-error formula say, and what exact one-sided 95% upper bound can you give instead?

Show answer

(a) Let $I_i$ be $1$ when episode $i$ contains at least one violation and $0$ otherwise. For independent episodes with a common violation probability $p$, these are Bernoulli variables and the sample proportion estimates $p$:

$$\hat p=\frac1{200}\sum_{i=1}^{200}I_i=\frac{14}{200}=0.07.$$

The true sampling variance of this average is $p(1-p)/200$. Replacing the unknown $p$ by $\hat p$ gives the estimated standard error

$$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}= \sqrt{\frac{0.07(1-0.07)}{200}} =\sqrt{\frac{0.07(0.93)}{200}} =\sqrt{0.0003255}\approx0.01804.$$

(b) The normal approximation uses about $1.96$ standard errors on either side. The half-width is $1.96(0.0180416)\approx0.0353616$, giving

$$0.07\pm0.0353616 \approx[0.0346384,\,0.1053616]\approx[0.035,\,0.105].$$

These are approximate sampling-based confidence limits, not an exact finite-sample interval or a posterior interval for a random $p$.

(c) Zero observed failures gives $\hat p=0$ and hence a plug-in standard error of zero. That boundary estimate does not establish certainty: positive true rates can still produce a clean sample. For any fixed $p$, the probability of $200$ clean independent episodes is $(1-p)^{200}$. The exact one-sided upper limit solves

$$ (1-p_U)^{200}=0.05,\qquad p_U=1-0.05^{1/200} =1-\exp\!\left(\frac{\ln0.05}{200}\right)\approx0.014867.$$

This is the one-sided Clopper–Pearson limit. The approximation $-\ln0.05\approx3$ explains the rule of three, $p_U\approx3/200=0.015$. The resulting confidence procedure covers the fixed rate in at least $95\%$ of repeated samples; zero failures in this sample does not prove a zero population rate.

exercises.label: Exercise C.2 — An alarm, a base rate and many steps

exercise.html:
Exercise C.2 — An alarm, a base rate and many steps

A change detector has false-alarm probability $0.01$ and detection probability $0.9$ per step, and a change occurs at a given step with prior probability $0.02$. (a) Compute $\mathbb P(\text{change}\mid\text{alarm})$. (b) Over $500$ steps without any change, how many false alarms do you expect, and what is the probability of at least one if the steps are independent? (c) Which per-step level keeps the probability of any false alarm in $500$ steps at most $0.05$ without assuming independence, and which two-sided Gaussian threshold on a standardised residual does it give?

Show answer

(a) Let $C$ mean a change and $A$ an alarm. The two joint alarm routes are $\mathbb P(C\cap A)=0.02(0.9)=0.018$ and $\mathbb P(C^c\cap A)=0.98(0.01)=0.0098$. Add them before conditioning:

$$\mathbb P(C\mid A)=\frac{0.018}{0.018+0.0098} =\frac{0.018}{0.0278}=\frac{90}{139}\approx0.647.$$

The false-alarm fraction among alarms is consequently $49/139\approx0.353$, about one in three. Sensitivity and posterior change probability have different denominators.

(b) With no change, define a false-alarm indicator at each step. Linearity of expectation gives an expected count $500(0.01)=5$, even without independence. Independence is needed for the next product: no false alarm has probability $0.99^{500}\approx0.0065705$. Thus

$$\mathbb P(\text{at least one false alarm})=1-0.99^{500}\approx0.99343.$$

exercises.label: Exercise C.3 — A Gaussian posterior and a safety probability

exercise.html:
Exercise C.3 — A Gaussian posterior and a safety probability

Prior $f\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$. Four measurements $y_i=f+\varepsilon_i$ with $\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.25)$ i.i.d. and independent of $f$ have mean $\bar y=0.9$. (a) Compute the posterior mean and variance with precision addition. (b) Compute $\mathbb P(f\lt0.5\mid\text{data})$. (c) Is $f\ge0.3$ certified by the lower bound $\mu-2\sigma$, and what is the posterior probability that this bound fails?

Show answer

(a) The four independent measurement noises each have variance $0.25$, so their average has variance $4(0.25)/4^2=0.25/4=0.0625=1/16$. Its precision is the reciprocal, $16$. The prior variance is $1$, hence prior precision $1$.

For independent Gaussian observations of the same $f$, precisions add and the mean is precision weighted:

$$s^2=(1+16)^{-1}=\frac1{17},\qquad m=\frac{1(0)+16(0.9)}{17}=\frac{14.4}{17}=\frac{72}{85}.$$

Thus $f\mid\text{data}\sim\mathcal N(72/85,1/17)$, with mean about $0.847059$, variance about $0.058824$, and standard deviation $s=1/\sqrt{17}\approx0.242536$. Each precision is inverse variance, not inverse standard deviation.

(b) Standardize the safety threshold using this posterior:

$$\mathbb P(f\lt0.5\mid\text{data}) =\Phi\!\left(\frac{0.5-72/85}{1/\sqrt{17}}\right) =\Phi(-1.430960\ldots)\approx0.07622.$$

(c) Evaluate the proposed lower bound before comparing it with $0.3$:

$$m-2s=\frac{72}{85}-\frac2{\sqrt{17}} \approx0.847059-0.485071=0.361988\gt0.3.$$

Therefore the $m-2s$ lower-bound rule certifies the proposed threshold under this posterior model. That lower bound fails exactly when $f\lt m-2s$, or $(f-m)/s\lt-2$, with posterior probability $\Phi(-2)\approx0.02275\approx0.023$. This is the failure probability of the displayed lower bound, rather than the probability of $f\lt0.3$. It is a Bayesian, model-dependent statement for this decision; multiple decisions need their joint failure event and risk allocation.

exercises.label: Exercise C.4 — How many runs, and which $R$?

exercise.html:
Exercise C.4 — How many runs, and which $R$?

Outcomes lie in $[0,1]$. (a) How many independent samples guarantee $|\bar X_N-m|\lt0.05$ with probability at least $0.99$, using Chebyshev with the worst-case variance and using Hoeffding? (b) Give a valid sub-Gaussian parameter for noise uniform on $[-0.2,0.2]$ and compare it with the standard deviation. (c) Why is noise uniform on $[0,0.2]$ not covered by (b)?

Show answer

(a) For $0\le X\le1$, we have $X^2\le X$. With mean $m$, this yields

$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-m^2 \le m-m^2=\frac14-(m-\tfrac12)^2\le\frac14.$$

Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_N)\le1/(4N)$. Chebyshev bounds the failure of the strict accuracy requirement by

$$\mathbb P(|\bar X_N-m|\ge0.05) \le\frac{1}{4N(0.05)^2}=\frac{100}{N}.$$

Require $100/N\le0.01$, so $N\ge10000$. Hoeffding instead gives $2e^{-2N(0.05)^2}=2e^{-0.005N}$. Solving $2e^{-0.005N}\le0.01$ gives $N\ge\ln(200)/0.005\approx1059.6635$, hence $N=1060$. These are sufficient sizes from the two bounds, using independent samples with the stated mean and range.

(b) A uniform error on $[-0.2,0.2]$ is centered. Hoeffding's lemma supplies $R=(0.2-(-0.2))/2=0.2$. Its variance is $(0.4)^2/12=1/75$, so its standard deviation is $\sigma=0.4/\sqrt{12}=0.2/\sqrt3\approx0.11547$.

The sharper claim in the section's table, that the smallest valid $R$ for this uniform law equals $\sigma$, can be checked explicitly. For a uniform $U$ on $[-a,a]$, integration gives the MGF $\mathbb E[e^{tU}]=\sinh(at)/(at)$, with value $1$ at $t=0$. Its power series obeys

$$\frac{\sinh(at)}{at} =\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{(a^2t^2)^j}{(2j+1)!} \le\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{(a^2t^2/6)^j}{j!} =e^{a^2t^2/6}.$$

The coefficient inequality uses $(2j+1)!\ge6^j j!$: starting at $j=0$, each next factor $(2j+2)(2j+3)$ is at least $6(j+1)$. All series terms are nonnegative. Thus $R=a/\sqrt3$ works, since $a^2t^2/6=R^2t^2/2$. No smaller value works: the second-order MGF terms are $1+a^2t^2/6+\cdots$ and $1+R^2t^2/2+\cdots$, requiring $R^2\ge a^2/3$. At $a=0.2$, Hoeffding's $0.2$ is conservative by the factor $\sqrt3$.

(c) A uniform error on $[0,0.2]$ has mean $0.1$, so it does not satisfy the uncentered zero-mean MGF condition used above. Write it as $0.1+\xi$, where $\xi$ is centered and uniform on $[-0.1,0.1]$. The bias must still appear in the observation model or be corrected separately; increasing a noise scale cannot make that mean vanish.

exercises.label: Exercise C.5 — KL, total variation and Pinsker

exercise.html:
Exercise C.5 — KL, total variation and Pinsker

Let $p=(0.6,0.3,0.1)$ and $q=(0.4,0.4,0.2)$. (a) Compute $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$, $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ and $d_{\rm TV}(p,q)$. (b) Check Pinsker's inequality in both directions. (c) For $q'=(0.5,0.5,0)$, which of $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q')$ and $\mathrm{KL}(q'\|p)$ is infinite, and what does that mean for a trust region?

Show answer

(a) All coordinates of $p$ and $q$ are positive. Using natural logarithms and the first law as weights,

$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{KL}(p\|q) &=0.6\ln\frac{0.6}{0.4}+0.3\ln\frac{0.3}{0.4}+0.1\ln\frac{0.1}{0.2}\\ &=0.6\ln1.5+0.3\ln0.75+0.1\ln0.5\\ &\approx0.243279-0.086305-0.069315=0.087660,\\ \mathrm{KL}(q\|p) &=0.4\ln\frac23+0.4\ln\frac43+0.2\ln2\\ &\approx-0.162186+0.115073+0.138629=0.091516. \end{aligned}$$

Both are in nats. Total variation is $d_{\rm TV}(p,q)=\tfrac12(|0.6-0.4|+|0.3-0.4|+|0.1-0.2|)=\tfrac12(0.2+0.1+0.1)=0.2$.

(b) TV is symmetric, so Pinsker can use either KL direction. Evaluating the bounds from the exact expressions gives

$$0.2\le\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)/2}\approx0.20936,\qquad 0.2\le\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)/2}\approx0.21391.$$

Both inequalities hold, although their upper bounds differ.

(c) The third coordinate contributes $0.1\ln(0.1/0)$ to $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q')$, hence this direction is infinite. In the reverse direction, the zero $q'$-weight contributes zero:

$$\mathrm{KL}(q'\|p)=0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.6} +0.5\ln\frac{0.5}{0.3} =0.5\ln\frac56+0.5\ln\frac53\approx0.164.$$

A finite constraint $\mathrm{KL}(\text{new}\|\text{old})\le\epsilon$ therefore forbids positive new-policy mass on an action with zero old-policy mass. The direction of the trust-region KL determines this support restriction.

exercises.label: Exercise C.6 — VaR, CVaR and the Gaussian shortcut

exercise.html:
Exercise C.6 — VaR, CVaR and the Gaussian shortcut

Episode costs are $Z\in\{0,2,10\}$ with probabilities $0.8,0.15,0.05$. (a) Compute $\mathbb E[Z]$, $\mathbb P(Z\gt0)$, $\operatorname{VaR}_{0.9}(Z)$ and $\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(Z)$, the latter both as a tail average and from Rockafellar–Uryasev at $\nu=\operatorname{VaR}_{0.9}$. (b) Compute $\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}$ of a Gaussian with the same mean and variance. (c) Which of $\mathbb E[Z]\le1$, $\mathbb P(Z\gt0)\le0.25$, $\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(Z)\le5$ hold?

Show answer

(a) Weight each possible cost by its probability:

$$\mathbb E[Z]=0.8(0)+0.15(2)+0.05(10)=0.3+0.5=0.8,\qquad \mathbb P(Z\gt0)=0.15+0.05=0.2.$$

The CDF has $F(0)=0.8$ and $F(2)=0.95$, so the first threshold reaching $0.9$ is $\operatorname{VaR}_{0.9}(Z)=2$. The worst $10\%$ of mass uses all $0.05$ at cost $10$ and another $0.05$ from the cost-$2$ atom:

$$\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(Z)=\frac{0.05(10)+0.05(2)}{0.1} =\frac{0.5+0.1}{0.1}=6.$$

In the Rockafellar–Uryasev formula, the multiplier is $1/(1-0.9)=10$. At $\nu=2$, only cost $10$ has positive excess, so

$$\nu+\frac{\mathbb E[(Z-\nu)^+]}{0.1} =2+\frac{0.05(10-2)}{0.1}=2+4=6.$$

(b) The second moment is $0.15(2^2)+0.05(10^2)=0.6+5=5.6$. Thus the variance is $5.6-0.8^2=4.96$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{4.96}\approx2.227106$.

For the Gaussian comparison law, let $q=\Phi^{-1}(0.9)$ and let $\varphi$ be the standard-normal density. Its upper $10\%$ corresponds to a standard-normal variable $W\ge q$. Since $\varphi'(w)=-w\varphi(w)$, integration gives $\int_q^\infty w\varphi(w)\,dw=\varphi(q)$. Dividing by the tail probability $0.1$ yields

$$\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.9}(\text{Gaussian}) =0.8+\sqrt{4.96}\frac{\varphi(\Phi^{-1}(0.9))}{0.1} \approx0.8+2.227106(1.754983)\approx4.71.$$

Here $q\approx1.2816$ and $\varphi(q)\approx0.175498$; these and the final value are approximations. Matching the mean and variance does not match the tail law: the Gaussian result is about $1.3$ below the actual discrete CVaR $6$.

(c) The actual mean constraint holds because $0.8\le1$, and the chance constraint holds because $0.2\le0.25$. The actual CVaR constraint fails because $6\gt5$. Using the Gaussian shortcut would incorrectly accept this last constraint, since its approximate $4.71$ is below $5$.

Matching the mean and variance does not match the tail law: the Gaussian result is about $1.3$ below the actual discrete CVaR $6$. Using the Gaussian shortcut would incorrectly accept this last constraint, since its approximate $4.71$ is below $5$.

exercise.html:
Exercise C.7 — Conformal coverage is itself random

Split conformal prediction uses $n=19$ calibration scores and one test score, all i.i.d. with a continuous law, and $\alpha=0.1$. (a) Which order statistic is the threshold, and what is the marginal coverage? (b) The coverage $C$ of one fixed calibration set is random: give its law, mean, standard deviation and $\mathbb P(C\lt0.8)$. (c) The coverage is measured on $m=2000$ fresh test points. What is the standard deviation of the measured coverage, and which source of randomness dominates?

Show answer

(a) Split conformal uses $k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$. Here $n=19$ and $\alpha=0.1$, so $k=\lceil20(0.9)\rceil=18$. The threshold is the $18$th smallest of the $19$ calibration scores, their second largest. Continuity prevents ties, and the future score has uniform rank among all $20$ scores. Acceptance is equivalent to rank at most $18$, giving marginal coverage $18/20=0.9$.

(b) Fix a realized calibration set. Its true conditional coverage is $C=F(S_{(18)})$, because a fresh independent score has CDF $F$. Across random calibration sets, the probability integral transform makes the $19$ values $F(S_i)$ independent uniforms. Since $F$ preserves their order, $C$ is their $18$th order statistic.

For $0\le c\le1$, the event $C\le c$ means at least $18$ of these $19$ uniforms lie below $c$. Count the cases of exactly $18$ and all $19$:

$$\mathbb P(C\le c)=\binom{19}{18}c^{18}(1-c)+c^{19} =19c^{18}-18c^{19}.$$

Differentiating gives density $342c^{17}(1-c)$ on $[0,1]$, the Beta$(18,2)$ law. Its first two moments can be obtained by elementary integration:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[C]&=342\int_0^1(c^{18}-c^{19})\,dc =342\left(\frac1{19}-\frac1{20}\right)=\frac9{10},\\ \mathbb E[C^2]&=342\int_0^1(c^{19}-c^{20})\,dc =342\left(\frac1{20}-\frac1{21}\right)=\frac{57}{70}. \end{aligned}$$

Thus $\operatorname{Var}(C)=57/70-(9/10)^2=3/700\approx0.004286$, and its standard deviation is $\sqrt{3/700}\approx0.06547$. Substituting $c=0.8$ into the CDF gives

$$\mathbb P(C\lt0.8)=19(0.8)^{18}(0.2)+(0.8)^{19} \approx0.08287\approx0.083.$$

The strict inequality has the same probability because this law is continuous. About one calibration set in twelve has true conditional coverage below $0.8$, despite the correct $0.9$ marginal coverage.

(c) Given the calibration set, its $m=2000$ fresh test acceptances are independent Bernoulli variables with probability $C$. Their measured fraction $\hat C$ therefore satisfies $\mathbb E[\hat C\mid C]=C$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\hat C\mid C)=C(1-C)/2000$. Across both calibration and test randomness, total variance gives

$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat C)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\frac{\mathbb E[C(1-C)]}{2000}.$$

The remaining expectation is $\mathbb E[C]-\mathbb E[C^2]=9/10-57/70=3/35$. Therefore

$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat C)=\frac3{700}+\frac{3/35}{2000} =\frac{300}{70000}+\frac3{70000}=\frac{303}{70000},\qquad \operatorname{SD}(\hat C)=\sqrt{\frac{303}{70000}}\approx0.0658.$$

The test-set contribution is only $1\%$ of the calibration variance. More test points estimate a fixed set's coverage more accurately, but do not remove the spread caused by using only $19$ calibration scores. The Beta calculation uses the supplied i.i.d. continuous score law; exchangeability alone would justify the marginal rank argument, but not this conditional-coverage law.
